chapter_theme: Poems 21-40 are court poems to three kings: the Pandya Nedunchezhiyan of Talaiyalanganam and his predecessor at Kanapper fort (21-26), the Chola Nalankilli (27-33) and the Chola Killivalavan (34-40), with one Chera (22). Victory poems that make the fort, the battle sacrifice and the burned enemy land into praise sit beside kaanchi poems that turn the same kings toward transience, the three aims and grace, and counsel poems that tie a king's victories to the plough, his umbrella to his subjects and his fame to easy access and sweet speech.

21.reading: The poet praises the Pandya who took Kanapper fort, whose moat, sky-high wall, star-like battlements and sunless guard forest made it as hard to win back as water that hot iron has drunk, and blesses his spear to flourish in fame while those who scorn him perish with their name.
21.nuance: The fort is described at length only to be the measure of the man who took it: every defence is listed and then cancelled by the single word கடந்த of the colophon and the poem's 'hard to recover'. வேங்கை மார்பின் (line 9) reads best as the name of the fort's lord, Vengaimarpan, made to grieve; taken as 'tiger-chested' it would describe the victor instead.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed praised is the taking of a fortified town, which is siege, though the colophon files it as the king's excellence

comparisons.tenor: the fort wall
the battlements
the fort, as hard to win back once lost

22.reading: The poet, having come to see the land of Mantharam Cheral Irumporai said to be like the world of the gods, praises his musth elephants at their posts, his moon-white umbrella under whose shade the unarmed sleep safe, his open war camp loud with the thumbai-crowned warriors' kuravai, and his giving to the kin of those who bring tribute, and says the king never wearies of leading his army into enemy land because he does not sleep.
22.nuance: The camp is called வாய் காவாது பரந்து பட்ட, spread wide with its entrance unguarded: the king's safety is shown by a camp that needs no watch, and the sleepers 'without a sword at their side' sleep under his guard. The closing turn makes his sleeplessness the reason the kingdom is heaven-like.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises a king's excellence in his calling as guardian and leader of a camp

comparisons.tenor: the elephant's head swarming with bees at its musth
the king's white umbrella
the camp's huts roofed with paddy and cane
the warriors' kuravai swelling
the land the king guards

23.reading: Kalladanar tells Nedunchezhiyan, the victor of Alankanam, that he has seen his work in the enemy country: fords churned by bathing elephants, fields stripped by his Murugan-like bowmen, guarded trees felled in every grove, fine houses burned, a land where even the foe says he will do more, and a forest turned to a waste where a doe with her fawn, her stag killed by a tiger, nibbles white velai flowers.
23.nuance: The closing picture is not drawn as a comparison, but a doe left with her young after the stag's death, eating the flowers of a frightening field, is placed exactly where the poem's catalogue of ruin ends; it reads as the enemy's widowed households without saying so. The poet presents the devastation as what he has seen on his way to the king (கண்டனென் வருவல்).

thinai_evidence.note: felling the guarded tree and burning the enemy's towns are the deeds of invasion

comparisons.tenor: the king's bowmen
the king's might

comparisons.vehicle: எழிற்கலை புலிப்பால் பட்டெனச் சிறுமறி தழீஇய தெறிநடை மடப்பிணை
comparisons.tenor: the bereaved households of the conquered land (a reading; not stated)

24.reading: Mangudi Kizhar pictures Nedunchezhiyan's land, where reapers cool off in the sea, fishermen drink and dance, and women drink palm, cane and screw-pine waters, names Evvi's Mizhalai and the Velir's Muthooru among his gains, blesses his star and curses his enemies', bids him live in joy among his warriors, suppliants and women, and closes with the saying that the only ones who truly lived are those whose fame stays when they die.
24.nuance: Sea-shore and field are run together on purpose: the reapers of the paddy plunge into the southern sea and the women drink 'three waters' and bathe in the 'three waters' (முந்நீர், the sea), so the Pandya land is shown as one where marutham and neythal meet. The joyful blessing is a setting for the closing maxim, which turns the poem toward kaanchi: enjoy, but be among those who 'did not go as the many go'.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the maxim that only lasting fame outlives death, the world that does not stay

comparisons.tenor: the warriors of old families who have grown old with the king

25.reading: Kalladanar tells Chezhiyan that when two allied kings came against him like the sun and the moon come down to earth together, he wasted them on the battlefield and took their drums, and asks whether his spear, which had broken firm ranks, did not stop short of further ruin when he saw the widowed women beating their breasts and shearing their dark hair.
25.nuance: The poem's turn is a question about the spear (சிதைதல் உய்ந்தன்றோ), and whether it means the spear itself escaped damage or was spared further slaughter at the sight of the widows is not certain; on the second reading the victory poem ends in the victor's restraint. The widows shearing their hair is the plain statement of what the same poet left as an image at the end of 23.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed is a pitched battle won against two kings and the seizing of their drums

comparisons.vehicle: உருகெழு ஞாயிறு நிலவுத்திகழ் மதியமொடு நிலஞ்சேர்ந் தாஅங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the two allied kings coming against him together
the widows' dark hair

26.reading: Mangudi Kizhar praises Chezhiyan, whose elephants clear the field like wind-driven ships on the sea, who killed kings and took their drums and cooked a battlefield sacrifice with crowned heads for a hearth, blood for water and bangled arms for ladles, and who also completed the Vedic sacrifices among learned Brahmins with kings serving him, and says his enemies must have done penance, since by being called his foes they now live in the other world.
26.nuance: The two sacrifices are set side by side with the same verb: அடுகளம் வேட்ட (he sacrificed the killing field) and வேள்வி முற்றிய (he completed the rite). The ending's compliment is grim: the enemies were lucky, because dying at his hand earned them heaven.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's excellence in both war and rite

comparisons.tenor: the elephants charging through the battlefield

comparisons.vehicle: முடித் தலை அடுப் பாகப் புனல் குருதி உலைக் கொளீஇத் தொடித்தோள் துடுப்பின்
comparisons.tenor: the battlefield as a sacrificial kitchen

27.reading: Among those born in flawless lines like the full hundred-petalled lotus and seated on thrones, the poet tells Nalankilli, few have fame in prose and song while many perish like lotus leaves; he has heard that those whom poets praise reach a sky-car no charioteer drives, so in this world where the moon shows everyone waning, waxing, dying and being born, Nalankilli should show grace to all who come in need, skilled or not, and leave ungiving to his enemies.
27.nuance: One plant gives both images: the full lotus flower for the few of noble birth who are remembered and its leaf, which rots unnoticed, for the many who are not. The moon's phases are offered as the plain proof of mortality that even the unlearned can see. The heaven-for-the-praised belief is reported as hearsay (என்ப ... எனக் கேட்பல்), not asserted by the poet.

thinai_evidence.note: the counsel rests on the world that does not stay

comparisons.tenor: the flawless noble line
the many who die unremembered
every life, which wanes, dies and is born

28.reading: Citing the ancients' saying that the eight defective births bring their bearers nothing but folly, the poet tells Nalankilli that his enemies now live in jungles where the jungle-cock wakes the millet-watchers, while his own heartland, where thrown cane-stalks crush lotus buds, looks like a dancers' floor; so his wealth can achieve virtue, wealth and pleasure, and failing to do so would be only his own neglect.
28.nuance: The argument seems to be that a man born whole and rich, unlike the eight kinds of defective birth, has no excuse: if the three aims are not achieved, the fault is his own neglect (போற்றாமை). The link between the opening list and the rest is compressed, and line 11 (புறஞ்சிறை மாக்கட்கு அறங்குறித்து) is hard to place, so this reading is offered with doubt.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is counsel addressed to the king, செவியறிவுறூஉ in kind, though the colophon names it a maxim kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the king's heartland strewn with cane and lotus

29.reading: The poet blesses Nalankilli: may bards throng his court, then women embrace him; may he punish the wicked and protect the good without slackening and never side with those who say good and evil bear no fruit; may his soldiers who enjoy his rich land and his deeds be kind to those who come; and in a world where people pass in turn like the players at a festival, may his kin be his joy and his stored wealth turn into fame.
29.nuance: The poem names and rejects a view: 'there is no good in good and no evil in evil' (lines 11, 12), a denial of moral consequence, so the anthology already knows such a doctrine to argue against it. Lines 17 to 22 are syntactically difficult, and whose kindness and whose small huts are meant is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the blessings rest on a world where all pass in turn

comparisons.tenor: the people of this world who pass one after another

30.reading: There are people who speak of the sun's path and motion, the circle it moves in, the quarters the wind blows and the empty sky as if they had gone and measured them, the poet tells Nalankilli, but his strength is hidden like the stone an elephant holds in its cheek, so how can poets sing it openly, lord of the land where great ships enter Puhar without striking mast or sail and pour out the sea's goods on the roads?
30.nuance: The praise works by contrast: the heavens can be measured, but this king cannot. The image of the elephant's cheek-stone (kept hidden until it is thrown) makes the hidden strength a weapon held back, not a lack.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is praise that declares the king beyond praise

comparisons.tenor: those who speak with certainty of the heavens
the king's concealed strength

31.reading: As wealth and pleasure follow behind virtue, the poet tells Nalankilli, the other two kings' umbrellas follow behind his single umbrella shining like the moon; seeking fame he will stay only in a war camp, his elephants never rest from charging forts, his warriors never call any land too far, and so the northern kings lie awake in dread that he will march round from the eastern sea to the western.
31.nuance: The opening simile takes the ordering of the three aims (virtue first, wealth and pleasure following) and uses it to rank the three crowned kings, so an ethical doctrine is made into the vehicle of a political claim. The march 'with the eastern sea behind' and the horses' hooves in the western surf is a circuit of conquest round the land.

thinai_evidence.note: the fear of the northern kings is fear of an invasion

comparisons.tenor: the two other kings' umbrellas following his
his single umbrella

32.reading: The poet calls the gift-seekers to come and sing Nalankilli with him, since he will give Vanji (a 'vanji that bears no flowers') to fill their cooking pots and towered Madurai so the viralis may get the price of flowers; and by ancient right this cool land is in his hand like the fresh clay the potter's boys set on the wheel.
32.nuance: பூவா வஞ்சி is a pun: not the flowering vanji creeper but the Chera capital Vanji. The potter's clay image says the land is his to shape as he likes; the generosity promised is a conquest promised.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem summons the gift-seekers to praise a giver

comparisons.vehicle: வேட்கோச் சிறாஅர் தேர்க்கால் வைத்த பசுமண் குரூஉத்திரள்
comparisons.tenor: the land in the king's hand

33.reading: Even in the Pandya's country, where the hunter's basket of venison and the herdgirl's pot of curds are filled with white paddy by the ploughmen's women, the poet tells Nalankilli, he broke the doors of seven forts and carved his tiger emblem, and his fierce war camp, where bards sing vanji and the bards' families are fed heaps of meat and rice like balls of unopened flowers, outdoes all the festivals he held in his flowering groves.
33.nuance: The opening shows the barter of three lands (hill meat, pasture curds, field paddy) as a picture of a settled, prosperous country, which makes the conquest larger. Lines 16 to 22 on the festival groves are hard to construe, and the subject of the doll simile and of the rams slaughtered at every gate is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's excellence in war and in feeding his people at the camp

comparisons.tenor: the heaps of meat and rice
the beauty of the festival dancers or lovers

34.reading: Dharma says there is expiation for those who cut a cow's udders, destroy women's unborn children or wrong their elders, but none, even if the earth is overturned, for those who kill a benefit; so, the poet tells Killivalavan, if he did not sing the king who made the bards rich after they ate millet with milk and honey and roast hare, the sun would not rise; and he blesses him to live more years than the drops the Himalayan rain-cloud pours.
34.nuance: The poem quotes a rule of dharma in order to apply it to the poet himself: not to praise his benefactor would be the one sin with no atonement. The poet calls himself தஞ்சம் (a humble, dependent man), and the cosmic oath (the sun would not rise) raises his debt of gratitude to the order of nature.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is the praise of a patron, framed as the poet's duty of gratitude

comparisons.tenor: the grains of varagu millet
the years wished for the king

35.reading: The poet tells Killivalavan that among the three Tamil kings kingship is his and the Kaveri-fed land is his, then counsels him: in the land of the just sceptre where the humble can reach the king when they seek justice, rain comes when it is sought; his tall umbrella is not for shade but to shelter suffering subjects; his victories are the fruit of the plough's furrow; the world blames kings when rains fail or harvests drop, so he should ignore the talk of malcontents, bear the burden of those who rear the plough-oxen and protect his people, and even the unsubmitting will bow at his feet.
35.nuance: Two causal claims carry the counsel: just rule brings rain, and victory in battle grows out of the furrow. The question about the umbrella (is it to keep off the sun? no) turns the most visible royal emblem into a duty of shelter. The poem also warns that kings are blamed even for drought, whether or not they caused it.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is counsel addressed to a king

comparisons.tenor: the white flowers of the jointed cane
the just sceptre

comparisons.vehicle: ஞாயிறு சுமந்த கோடுதிரள் கொண்டுமூ மாக விசும்பின் நடுவுநின்
comparisons.tenor: the king's wide umbrella
the elephants lying dead on the battlefield

36.reading: Whether he kills or releases the enemy, the poet tells Killivalavan, he knows his own worth: while the sound of his smiths' axes felling the guarded trees on the Porunai's banks, where girls once played with gold stones on the sand, echoes into the walled palace where the other king sits at ease, and Valavan's drum roars here, to say he fought such a king is a matter of shame.
36.nuance: The poem praises by rebuke: it says nothing against the siege's power, only that a king who will not come out is no fit opponent, so the honour of continuing the war is gone. The girls' play on the river sand, ruined by the felling, is a small picture of what the war destroys.

thinai_evidence.note: the felling of the guarded trees of another king's land is the work of an invading army

37.reading: Descendant of the Chembiyan who relieved a bird's distress, with an army that strikes like the thunderbolt that hits the hill cleft a five-headed cobra has entered, the poet tells Killivalavan, he is able to wreck in battle the old town walled like copper, with its crocodile-filled moat where the beasts snap at the torch-shadows of the night watch, without sparing it as 'fine', because a king with decked elephants is inside.
37.nuance: Lineage and conduct are set against each other: the king is first named by his ancestor's famous mercy to a bird, and then praised for showing no mercy to a fine old town, because a rival king shelters in it. The poem neither blames nor excuses the destruction.

colophon.thurai: அரச வாகை குற்றுழிஞை எனவும், முதல் வஞ்சி எனவும் பாடம்

thinai_evidence.note: the deed is the storming of a walled and moated town

comparisons.tenor: the king's army striking the foe sheltering in his fort
the town's wall

38.reading: The poet tells Killivalavan, whose angry glance spreads fire and whose loving glance makes gold bloom, and who could bring moonlight out of the sun or sunshine out of the moon, that those born and raised in his shade cannot measure him, and that gift-seekers even in enemy lands think of his country, because heaven, where people only enjoy what their deeds earned and where no one gives or asks, is lacking, while here the same enjoyment is had along with giving.
38.nuance: The poem ranks the king's land above heaven on one ground: in heaven there is neither giving nor asking, so the gift-relation itself, which bards live by, is what earth has that heaven lacks. The comparison of the two worlds is put in the bards' mouths.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is praise of a king as the giver bards long for

comparisons.tenor: the young elephants
the swaying flags

39.reading: Descendant of the king who entered the ivory-beamed scale for a dove's sake, the poet tells Killivalavan, giving is not his own fame; with ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort, killing is not his fame; with justice standing firm in the Chola court at Urantai, justice is not his fame; so how can he praise him, except by singing the might that withered the unwithering Vanji when the Chera of the Himalaya-carved bow fell?
39.nuance: Each inherited virtue is set aside as the family's, not his, which leaves one deed that is his alone: the defeat of the Chera. வாடா வஞ்சி வாட்டும் is a pun, the vanji (creeper, and the Chera capital) that does not wither, made to wither.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is praise that searches for what is the king's own

comparisons.tenor: the king's shoulders

40.reading: The poet tells Killivalavan, who took others' guarded forts and wears anklets made of the gold of their crowns, that his poets wish to see him always as today, so that his detractors bow their necks and his praisers shine, and asks him to be sweet of speech and easy to reach, lord of the land where the small spot one cow-elephant lies on feeds seven bull elephants.
40.nuance: The counsel is two words long, இன்சொல் and எண்பதம் (ease of access), and it is given to a conqueror at the height of his strength, as the condition for his praise lasting.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is counsel to a king

links.note: Kural 743 defines a fort by height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility; 21 describes Kanapper with a moat beyond depth, a sky-high wall and a sunless guard forest, and praises the king who took it.
links.teaches: The puram poet uses the full list of what makes a fort good only to measure the man who took it, so the Kural's criteria guarantee nothing to the defender: in the praise poem a perfect fort is the conqueror's ornament.

links.note: Both by Kalladanar to Nedunchezhiyan: 23 ends on a doe and fawn whose stag the tiger has killed; 25 ends on widows beating their breasts and shearing their hair.
links.teaches: The same poet states openly in 25 what 23 leaves as a bare image, which supports reading the bereaved doe of 23 as the enemy's widows and shows that a puram poet could move between the hidden and the stated forms of one grief.

links.note: 23 praises the victor of Alankanam; Akananuru 175 compares the lightning of the returning rains to the spear Chezhiyan raised after winning at Alankanam.
links.teaches: The heroine's speech in an akam poem borrows the Pandya's Alankanam victory, which 23 celebrates as fact, to measure the flashing of the rains that mark her lover's promised return, so a war became a stock image of brilliance within the poets' own generation.

links.note: 24 names the Mizhalai of Evvi, the generous Vel, among the lands Chezhiyan holds; Akananuru 266 names Evvi of Needur, true of sword, and the uproar after his men's victory.
links.teaches: One chief is remembered in the Purananuru for open-handed giving and for lands that passed to the Pandya, and in the Akananuru as a byword for the din of his war victory, so the akam poets kept a lesser king's martial name alive as a measure of loud gossip.

links.note: 24 ends: those who knew say the ones who truly lived are those who did not go as the many go but stood and died with lasting fame; Kural 240 says those who live without renown do not live.
links.teaches: The Kural's flat verdict appears in 24 as a saying the poet attributes to the wise and sets after a blessing of royal pleasure, so the maxim was already proverbial and served to bend a feast poem toward the thought of death.

links.note: 26 calls Chezhiyan அடுகளம் வேட்ட, the one who sacrificed the killing field; Akananuru 36 measures the town's gossip by the roar when Chezhiyan at Alankanam களம்வேட்ட, after killing seven kings in one day.
links.teaches: The same phrase for the battlefield sacrifice appears in a praise poem and in a heroine's quarrel with her husband, which shows the Pandya's war rite was famous enough as a phrase to serve an akam speaker as the loudest noise she could name.

links.note: 27 line 6 மரைஇலை போல மாய்ந்திசினோர் பலரே (many died like the lotus leaf); Naladiyar 359 ends மரையிலையின் மாய்ந்தார் பலர் (many perished like the lotus leaf).
links.teaches: The Naladiyar repeats the Purananuru's half-line almost word for word but moves it from nobly born kings who died without a poet's praise to people whose expectations came to nothing, and the earlier poem shows what the lotus-leaf death meant: dying without a name, beside the flower that is remembered.

links.note: 27 reports the saying that those whom poets praise reach a sky-car that no charioteer drives; Kural 234 says that if one wins long fame on earth, the gods' world does not honour the புலவர்.
links.teaches: The belief that poets' praise carries a man to heaven, which 27 gives as current hearsay, is the background the elliptical couplet assumes when it ties earthly fame to the gods' world, so the Purananuru supplies the premise the Kural leaves out.

links.note: 28 tells the king his wealth can achieve virtue, wealth and pleasure, and failure would be his own neglect; Kural 754 says wealth gained by right means without wrong yields virtue and pleasure.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the yield of virtue and pleasure depend on how wealth was gained, while the court poet makes it depend on whether the king takes care to use it, so the two books place the moral test of wealth at opposite ends, getting and spending.

links.note: 29 sets its blessing in a world where people pass in turn like players at a festival; Kural 332 likens wealth's coming and going to a crowd that gathers at a dance hall and disperses.
links.teaches: Both books reach for the festival stage to show transience, but the Purananuru applies it to the players, the people themselves, and draws the counsel to turn stored wealth into fame, while the Kural applies it to the audience, wealth itself, so the same image grounds two different lessons about what passes.

links.note: 31 opens: as wealth and pleasure follow behind virtue, so the two other kings' umbrellas follow behind Nalankilli's; Kural 39 says only what comes through virtue is joy.
links.teaches: The ordering the Kural states as an ethical rule is used by the court poet as a ready image to rank three crowned kings, which shows the precedence of virtue over wealth and pleasure was a commonplace secure enough to carry a political claim.

links.note: 34 quotes dharma: there is expiation for killing cows' udders, destroying unborn children or wronging elders, but none for killing a benefit; Kural 110 says those who killed any good may escape, but not one who killed a good done to him.
links.teaches: The Kural compresses into a rule what the Purananuru presents as a known saying with its list of lesser crimes, and the poet turns it on himself, so the maxim was already used to bind a bard to praise his patron: gratitude here is the poet's own obligation, not only the patron's claim.

links.note: 35 says the king's umbrella is for sheltering his people and his victories are the fruit of the plough's furrow; Kural 1034 says those with the shade of grain-ears see many kings' umbrellas under their own king's umbrella.
links.teaches: Both texts set the royal umbrella against the farmer and make conquest depend on the plough, but 35 says it to the king as counsel while the Kural says it of the farmer as praise, so the same economic claim is spoken from both ends of the realm.

links.note: 35 says rain comes when sought in the land of the just sceptre, but also that the world blames kings for failed rains and harvests; Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules rightly.
links.teaches: The Kural states the link between just rule and rain as a fact, while the court poet adds that people will blame the king for drought whatever its cause, so in the Purananuru the doctrine is also a political danger the king must manage.

links.note: 36 tells the besieging king that to have fought a rival who sits at ease behind his walls is a matter of shame; Naladiyar 241 says the worthy, seeing their enemies humbled, feel shame and do not advance.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's maxim about shame before a humbled foe is in 36 an actual plea to stop a siege, which shows the poets used this sense of honour to bring wars to an end, and that the shame was felt to fall on the victor.

links.note: Both by Nappasalaiyar to Killivalavan open by naming him the descendant of the Chola who relieved a dove's distress (37 புள்ளுறு புன்கண் தீர்த்த; 39 the king who entered the scale for the dove).
links.teaches: The poet uses one ancestral legend of mercy in opposite ways: in 37 it heads praise of a king who spares no fine town, and in 39 it is set aside as inherited fame that cannot be his own, so the legend served both to honour the line and to ask what the living king had added.

links.note: 38 says heaven lacks giving and asking, so gift-seekers prefer the king's land; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
links.teaches: Both books cut the worth of giving loose from heaven, but from opposite sides: the Kural says giving is good even without a heaven to reward it, and the Purananuru says heaven is poorer than earth because no one gives there, so giving becomes what makes this world worth more than the next.

links.note: 40 asks the conqueror to be sweet of speech and easy of access (இன்சொல் எண்பதத்தை); Kural 386 says the land of a king easy to see and not harsh of speech is praised above others.
links.teaches: The Kural's two marks of a praised king are in 40 exactly the two requests a poet puts to a victorious king, so the couplet's criteria were the counsel bards gave in person, and the poem ties them to the king's fame among his poets.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: பரிசில் மாக்கள் in 32 line 6 and பரிசிலர் in 38 line 17

source_issues: 22 line 38: சோறுயட looks like the review's யடு-for-யொடு fault (சோறொடு), though the sense of the line ('leading the army with food') is uncertain either way; marked as it stands.
24 line 8: கன்ணி is a misprint for கண்ணி; line 18 ஒம்பா for ஓம்பா.
